title: Side effects & effect handlers
scopeHtml: Scope: why side effects need handlers, the effect APIs (LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, produceState, rememberCoroutineScope, rememberUpdatedState, snapshotFlow, derivedStateOf), keys, ordering, one-off events, lifecycle-aware collection and testing. Version notes: lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.6.0+ for collectAsStateWithLifecycle; compose-runtime artifacts are shown as 1.12.x on the current docs page (verify against your BOM); effect semantics below have been stable since Compose 1.0.

questions.promptHtml: Composable functions are supposed to be side-effect free. So how do you do real work like showing a snackbar, starting a network call or registering a listener from Compose, and why can't you just do it in the function body?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand that a composable body is a pure description that the runtime may run many times, out of order, or throw away.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A composable can run on every recomposition, can be skipped, can run in a different order, and a recomposition can be discarded if state changes mid-way. So anything in the body can execute zero, one or many times with no guarantee it ever 'committed'. Effect APIs (LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, and so on) run after the composition is applied, are tied to the composable's identity in the tree, and are cancelled or disposed when it leaves. That gives side effects a predictable lifecycle."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A composable is a function from state to UI description. The runtime reserves the right to:

  • re-execute it any number of times (recomposition),
  • skip it entirely when inputs are unchanged,
  • run it in a different order or (in future) in parallel,
  • abandon a composition pass whose snapshot became stale.

If you call analytics.log("screen_viewed") in the body, it logs on every recomposition, and may log for a pass that never reached the screen. Effects fix this by splitting "describe" from "act":

composition pass (may be discarded)   ->  apply changes (commit)  ->  effects run
  body executes, records effects          tree/slot table updated      LaunchedEffect coroutine starts
                                                                       SideEffect lambda runs
                                                                       onDispose of old effects first

Effects are bound to the call site's position in the slot table (see positional memoization in the C1 chunk). Same position + same keys = same effect instance continues. Leaves composition = cancelled/disposed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: runs on every recomposition, even discarded ones
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: ScreenViewModel) {
    vm.trackScreenView() // side effect in composition
    Content()
}

// Correct: runs once per entry into composition
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: ScreenViewModel) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.trackScreenView() }
    Content()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing "my screen only recomposes once so it's fine". Any state read (even an animation) multiplies calls.
  • Using an effect to do what an event handler (onClick) should do. Effects react to composition, handlers react to input.
  • Treating the effect body as "main thread, once". It is a coroutine, and it restarts when keys change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Name the effect APIs and one use for each → LaunchedEffect: suspend work; DisposableEffect: register/unregister; SideEffect: publish state to non-Compose code after each successful recomposition; produceState: non-Compose source to State; rememberCoroutineScope: launch from callbacks.
  2. Is it OK to mutate a MutableState directly in the body? → Writing state you also read in the same composition (a "backwards write") can cause recomposition loops; use an effect or derive the value instead.
  3. What guarantees does "after apply" give? → Effects see the committed tree; if the pass is discarded, the effect never ran.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "side effects go in LaunchedEffect". Senior: explains the runtime freedom (skip/reorder/discard), identity by call site, that effects run post-apply on the composition's dispatcher, and that most "effects" people write are really event handlers or derivations that should not be effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen-view event fired 3-9 times per open because an animated header recomposed the parent; dashboards showed 4x inflated funnel numbers until the call moved into a keyed LaunchedEffect.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how LaunchedEffect works. What do the keys do, and what happens on recomposition, on key change and when the composable leaves the composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LaunchedEffect is the most used effect and the most misused; keys are where most bugs come from.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine in a scope tied to its position in the composition when it enters. On recomposition with the same keys nothing happens, the coroutine keeps running. If any key changes, the old coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts. If it leaves the composition, the coroutine is cancelled. Keys compare with equals."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LaunchedEffect(key1) { ... } is a composable that remembers a LaunchedEffectImpl (a RememberObserver) keyed on the keys. When the observer is remembered (after apply) it calls scope.launch(block), where scope is created from the composition's effect coroutine context (Recomposer's context: Android main dispatcher plus the MonotonicFrameClock, which is why withFrameNanos and animateTo work inside it). On forgotten/abandoned it cancels the job.

enter composition ──► launch coroutine (key=A)
recompose, key=A  ──► nothing (same instance)
recompose, key=B  ──► cancel job(A) ──► launch job(B)
leave composition ──► cancel job

Multiple keys are all compared; any one changing restarts. LaunchedEffect() with no keys is not allowed (compile error: at least one key required, so people pass Unit/true).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun UserHeader(userId: String, vm: ProfileViewModel) {
    // Reloads when userId changes, cancels the in-flight load of the old user.
    LaunchedEffect(userId) {
        vm.load(userId)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• LaunchedEffect(Unit) while reading a changing parameter inside: the effect keeps the first value (stale capture, see the rememberUpdatedState question).
  • Heavy CPU work directly in the block: it runs on the main-ish effect dispatcher; switch with withContext(Dispatchers.Default).
  • Assuming the coroutine survives configuration change. It does not; the composition is torn down.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if load is not cooperative with cancellation? → The old one keeps running until it checks; two loads may race, so make the call suspend/cancellable.
  2. Does the effect run before the first frame? → It starts after the first composition is applied, so first frame may draw before it executes.
  3. What context does the block run on? → The composition's effect context (main thread dispatcher with a frame clock), not Dispatchers.Default.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: keys restart the effect. Senior: describes the RememberObserver mechanism, frame-clock context, cancellation cooperation, key equality semantics and that the first frame may precede the effect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen launched repo.search(query) with LaunchedEffect(Unit): results never updated after the first query. The fix was one word, the key.

questions.promptHtml: What does SideEffect do and when would you use it instead of LaunchedEffect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the one non-suspending effect and the "publish state outward" use case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SideEffect runs its lambda after every successful recomposition of that composable, not in a coroutine and not keyed. I use it to publish Compose state to something outside Compose, like setting a user property on an analytics object or updating a non-Compose view holder. If I need suspend calls or want it to run only on key change, I use LaunchedEffect."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: SideEffect registers the lambda to run in the apply phase after the composition is committed, on the composition thread. It re-registers on each recomposition of its scope; if the scope is skipped it does not run. Discarded passes never run it, which is its whole advantage over writing the call in the body. It has no cleanup. There are no keys: if you need "only when X changed", compare inside, or use a keyed effect.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun TrackUserType(analytics: Analytics, user: User) {
    SideEffect {
        analytics.setUserProperty("userType", user.userType)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing network or disk work in SideEffect: it blocks the main thread and runs on every recomposition.
  • Expecting it to run when the parent recomposes but this scope is skipped: it will not.
  • Using it as a "once" hook.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference vs body call? → Body call can run for abandoned passes; SideEffect only after commit.
  2. Can SideEffect write Compose state? → Technically yes but it triggers another recomposition; usually a smell.
  3. Where does Compose itself use it? → Patterns like rememberSystemUiController-style libraries and BackHandler update their callback holders through it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "runs every recomposition". Senior: explains the commit guarantee, absence of keys and cancellation, and chooses it only to mirror state outward.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom player controller needed the current "isVisible" flag; it was set in the body and flickered when a pass was abandoned during fast scroll. Moving to SideEffect stopped phantom pauses.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use rememberCoroutineScope and when LaunchedEffect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic "two ways to launch a coroutine" question; it tests understanding of composition-driven vs event-driven work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LaunchedEffect is for work that should happen because of composition or a state/key change. rememberCoroutineScope gives me a scope I can use from callbacks like onClick, where I can't call a composable. Both are cancelled when the composable leaves the composition; the scope is created once per call site and I launch into it on demand."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Composable functions can only be called during composition, so event handlers cannot call LaunchedEffect. rememberCoroutineScope() returns a CoroutineScope remembered at the call site (cancelled when it leaves) whose context is the composition's effect context. Launching inside it creates children that live until cancellation or completion. Unlike LaunchedEffect, it does not restart on anything; each launch is independent, so two quick clicks can start two jobs unless you guard.

LaunchedEffect rememberCoroutineScope
Trigger composition / key change your callback
Restart on key change never, you manage Jobs
Callable from onClick no yes
Cleanup cancel on leave/key change cancel on leave

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Screen(host: SnackbarHostState) {
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    Button(onClick = {
        scope.launch { host.showSnackbar("Saved") }
    }) { Text("Save") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling scope.launch directly in the composable body (runs every recomposition).
  • Using a ViewModel scope for snackbar display, which outlives the UI.
  • Forgetting double-click guards; showSnackbar suspends until dismissed, so a second launch queues.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not viewModelScope.launch for the snackbar? → The snackbar host is UI; the scope must die with the UI. Business logic belongs in the ViewModel.
  2. What happens to a running job when the user navigates away? → Cancelled when the composable leaves the composition.
  3. Can you pass the scope into a long-lived object? → Avoid; it captures the composition and is cancelled with it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "one is for callbacks". Senior adds job overlap handling, relation to composition lifetime, and avoids hoisting scopes into state holders without understanding cancellation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-tapping "Place order" launched two coroutines that both called the same suspend API because the scope was used without a guard; moved to a ViewModel intent with idempotency.

questions.promptHtml: What is DisposableEffect for, and why does it require onDispose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you clean up registrations, which is the leak source in Compose code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "DisposableEffect is for effects that need teardown: registering and unregistering a listener, observer, receiver or callback. Its block runs when it enters or when keys change, and must end with onDispose { }, which runs when keys change or it leaves the composition. The compiler forces onDispose so you can't forget the cleanup."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Implemented as a RememberObserver: onRemembered runs the block and stores the DisposableEffectResult; onForgotten/onAbandoned calls dispose(). On key change the old result is disposed first, then the new block runs (within the same apply, disposals before additions, so you do not briefly hold two registrations). Not a coroutine: do not suspend; launch if needed. The block runs synchronously on the composition thread, so keep it quick.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun OnLifecycle(owner: LifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current, onEvent: (Lifecycle.Event) -> Unit) {
    val current by rememberUpdatedState(onEvent)
    DisposableEffect(owner) {
        val obs = LifecycleEventObserver { _, e -> current(e) }
        owner.lifecycle.addObserver(obs)
        onDispose { owner.lifecycle.removeObserver(obs) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Empty onDispose {}: hides a leak; reconsider the API.
  • Missing the owner/target as key; a changed owner leaves the observer on the old object.
  • Capturing a changing callback without rememberUpdatedState, then re-registering on each change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not LaunchedEffect with try/finally? → It works for suspend lifecycles but callbacks and listeners are not coroutine-shaped; onDispose is synchronous and explicit.
  2. Does onDispose run on process death? → No, only composition teardown.
  3. LocalLifecycleOwner location? → Moved to androidx.lifecycle.compose in recent lifecycle versions (verify for your version); the older compose-ui one is deprecated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: registers and unregisters. Senior: explains ordering with key change, why the lambda capture needs rememberUpdatedState, and audits for empty dispose.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A receiver registered in a bare LaunchedEffect leaked per navigation; LeakCanary showed the Activity retained 14 times after a QA session.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does rememberUpdatedState solve, and how is it different from adding the value as an effect key?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know "keys restart" from people who know how to keep a long-lived effect fresh without restarting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A long-running effect captures values when it starts. If a lambda parameter changes later, the effect still calls the old one. rememberUpdatedState returns a State that always holds the latest value; the effect reads it at call time. Adding the value as a key instead would cancel and restart the effect, which is wrong when restarting is expensive or semantically wrong, like a splash timer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
It is remember { mutableStateOf(v) }.apply { value = v }: the write happens during each composition, so the State holds the newest value. Reading .value inside the effect (at invocation time, not capture time) gets the latest. The State read in a coroutine is not a composition read, so reading it does not cause recomposition.

t0 compose onTimeout=A  -> effect starts, holds State(ref)
t1 recompose onTimeout=B -> State.value = B  (effect NOT restarted)
t2 effect fires          -> reads State.value -> B   (correct)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Splash(onTimeout: () -> Unit) {
    val current by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(2_000)
        current()           // latest lambda, timer never restarted
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it for values that should restart the effect (a userId). Those are keys.
  • Reading onTimeout directly (captured) after wrapping; you must read through the delegate inside the block.
  • Overusing it for everything, hiding real dependencies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. With strong skipping and remembered lambdas, is it still needed? → Yes; lambdas change identity when captured values change, and the effect still holds the first.
  2. Is there a thread-safety concern? → The write is in composition, the read in the effect on the same dispatcher by default; if you switch dispatchers, State reads are still snapshot-safe for latest-value use.
  3. Compare to derivedStateOf → That computes from state; this just carries a parameter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "wraps a lambda so it's up to date". Senior: explains capture-time vs call-time reads, restart cost trade-off and when a key is the right answer instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "session expired" countdown called a stale onExpired that referenced a previous user's navigator, causing a navigation to a dead destination.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout screen shows a 10-second "confirming payment" overlay. QA reports that after switching the payment method mid-wait, the wrong method is submitted about 5% of the time. Crash rate is zero; the bug appears only on slow devices. The code:

@Composable
fun ConfirmOverlay(method: PaymentMethod, onConfirm: (PaymentMethod) -> Unit) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(10_000)
        onConfirm(method)
    }
    OverlayContent(method)
}

The UI shows the new method after a switch, so the screen looks right.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it only appears sometimes, and fix it. What would you add to prevent this class of bug?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add method as a key." That restarts the 10-second timer on every change, which changes product behavior (user can extend the wait indefinitely), and does not explain why only UI looks right.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should switching method reset the 10-second wait (product)? Is method hoisted from a ViewModel or local state? Does the lambda onConfirm also change (e.g. captures a navigator)? Are there analytics around which method was shown vs submitted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage; ship a hotfix that submits from the ViewModel's current state instead of a UI-captured value, behind the same release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stale capture in the Unit-keyed effect; (b) ViewModel not updating state; (c) race in the repository. The red herring is "UI looks right": the composable body recomposes and shows the new method, but the running coroutine closed over the first value.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log method at effect start and at onConfirm; add a unit/UI test using mainClock.autoAdvance = false, change method, advance 10 s, assert the callback argument. Lint: Compose lint flags unused-key/stale captures only partly, so review manually.
  5. Root cause: LaunchedEffect(Unit) starts once. The lambda block captured method and onConfirm at first composition. Later recompositions create a new lambda but the running coroutine ignores it. "Sometimes" because it needs a change during the 10 s window; slow devices have more reasons for the user to tap again.
  6. Fix: short-term: val currentMethod by rememberUpdatedState(method) and val currentConfirm by rememberUpdatedState(onConfirm), read inside after the delay. If product wants the timer reset, key on method instead. Long-term: do not carry payment state in the UI; the ViewModel confirms what it holds.
  7. Prevention: a review checklist "every captured variable in an effect is a key or rememberUpdatedState" (the official guidance), a test for effect + state change, and treat LaunchedEffect(Unit) as a flag in review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not key on method without confirming product intent; I would not remove the delay by making confirmation instant.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if onConfirm is a ViewModel method reference (stable)? → Then the stale risk is only method; still use updated state or read from VM.
  • Would snapshotFlow { method } help? → Only if you must react to changes; for a single read at end, rememberUpdatedState is simpler.
  • Strong skipping on/off changes this? → No, stability affects skipping, not effect capture.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout team spent two sprints chasing a "backend race" before someone logged inside the effect and saw the first-composition value. The root fix was a three-line rememberUpdatedState and a PR template line.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: puts method as a key without considering the timer semantics or cannot explain why UI looks right.
  • Hire: identifies stale capture, uses rememberUpdatedState, asks about product intent.
  • Strong hire: also moves the decision to the ViewModel, writes the mainClock test, and adds the review checklist.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide the keys for an effect? Is LaunchedEffect(Unit) or LaunchedEffect(true) ever correct?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Key choice is the main source of effect bugs; the answer shows whether you reason about dependencies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Every value the effect block reads that should cause a restart on change must be a key. Values that shouldn't restart it go through rememberUpdatedState. A constant key like Unit means 'run once for the lifetime of this call site', which is valid for splash timers or one-time loads, but the docs call it as suspicious as while(true): it must be a deliberate choice."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rule of thumb: parameters/state read in the block are keys, unless they are remembered with no keys (never change) or wrapped in rememberUpdatedState. Keys compare with equals; an unstable or new-every-time key (a new List instance, a lambda created each composition without remember) restarts the effect on each recomposition. Under-keying causes stale behavior; over-keying causes repeated work and cancelled in-flight requests.

Situation Keys
Load data for id id
Observe lifecycle owner owner
Timer that must not restart Unit + rememberUpdatedState
Depends on a list's content stable id/hash, not the instance

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Config                                   // no equals(): identity comparison

LaunchedEffect(Config()) { apply() }           // broken: new instance each composition -> restarts every time
LaunchedEffect(config.version) { apply() }     // fine: cheap, stable primitive key
LaunchedEffect(items) { sync(items) }          // List.equals is content-based: no restart for equal lists, but O(n) per recomposition

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keying on an object type with identity equals that is rebuilt each composition.
  • Keying on a State object instead of its value (the State instance never changes, so no restart).
  • Using Unit and reading changing params.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Key on a MutableState or its value? → Its value; the state holder is the same instance.
  2. What happens to the old effect when keys change? → Cancelled (LaunchedEffect) or disposed (DisposableEffect) before the new one starts.
  3. When key is a data class with a large list? → equals is O(n) every recomposition; prefer a version number or id.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "put what you use in keys". Senior: separates restart-worthy from fresh-read values, knows equals cost and identity pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A key built from Modifier equality... was recreated each time; fixed by using a primitive id key and cutting 40 duplicate requests per screen open.

questions.promptHtml: What does produceState do, how is it built, and when do you prefer it over LaunchedEffect plus mutableStateOf?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of how non-Compose sources (callbacks, suspend loads) bridge into State, and that effects compose.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "produceState launches a composition-scoped coroutine that pushes values into a State it returns. Under the hood it's remember { mutableStateOf(initial) } plus a LaunchedEffect on the keys. It's a tidy way to wrap a suspend load or a callback API (with awaitDispose for teardown) into a State that composables can read. Use it for small adapters; for real screen data I'd hold the state in a ViewModel."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Keys restart the producer: cancel then relaunch, with the old value retained until the new one is produced (State keeps last value). Setting an equal value does not recompose (conflation via structural equality, the default policy). For callback sources, awaitDispose { unregister } suspends forever and runs cleanup on cancellation, so you do not need DisposableEffect.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun connectivity(cm: ConnectivityManager): State<Boolean> =
    produceState(initialValue = true, cm) {
        val cb = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
            override fun onAvailable(n: Network) { value = true }
            override fun onLost(n: Network) { value = false }
        }
        cm.registerDefaultNetworkCallback(cb)
        awaitDispose { cm.unregisterNetworkCallback(cb) }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting awaitDispose for callbacks (leak) or putting the registration outside the keys.
  • Using produceState for state that must survive rotation: it does not.
  • Naming a returning composable with an uppercase first letter (lint: should be camelCase).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Initial value problem? → Must be supplied; it renders until the first produce.
  2. Flow input? → Prefer collectAsStateWithLifecycle; produceState collecting a Flow is not lifecycle-aware.
  3. Error handling? → An uncaught exception inside the producer propagates to the composition's effect scope and can crash; catch inside.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: converts callbacks to state. Senior: knows it is composed of remember+LaunchedEffect, handles teardown via awaitDispose, and lists survivability limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A connectivity banner used produceState with no unregister; each navigation re-registered a callback until the system threw TooManyRequestsException at ~100 registrations.

questions.promptHtml: What does snapshotFlow do, and how is it different from collecting a state in the composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes the bridge from Compose state into coroutines/Flow and why you would avoid recomposition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "snapshotFlow turns reads of Compose State inside its block into a cold Flow. When collected, it runs the block, records which State objects were read, and re-runs when any of them changes, emitting the result if it is not equal to the previous emission. Because it works in the effect rather than the composition, state changes do not recompose anything, so it's ideal for scroll-position analytics or debouncing a text field."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Collection runs the block in a read-observing snapshot; on a global snapshot apply that touches a read State, the flow re-evaluates (on the collector's dispatcher). Output goes through distinctUntilChanged semantics via equals. Multiple writes in one frame are coalesced: you may miss intermediate values, so it is conflated, not a log of every change. It is cold: each collector has its own observation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val listState = rememberLazyListState()
LaunchedEffect(listState) {
    snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }
        .map { it > 0 }
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .collect { scrolledPast -> analytics.log("scrolled_past_first", scrolledPast) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading non-State values (plain vars) in the block: no re-evaluation.
  • Using it for UI that should just be derived in composition.
  • Expecting every intermediate value (typing fast) to be delivered.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why collect in a LaunchedEffect keyed on the state holder? → Collection is a suspend op; restarts correctly if the holder changes.
  2. snapshotFlow vs derivedStateOf? → See the comparison question; one yields Flow for effects, the other State for composition.
  3. Threading? → Evaluation occurs when the global snapshot applies; collector's dispatcher runs the flow operators.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: state to flow. Senior: explains conflation, snapshot observation, equality filtering and that it is for side-effect pipelines, not UI derivation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scroll-based "viewed" impression logged once per row via snapshotFlow with distinctUntilChanged reduced duplicate events by ~60% compared with logging in item composition.

questions.contextHtml:
A feed app (800k DAU) shipped a new "recommended for you" card. Backend p95 latency on /recs doubled and the server team reports each user opening the feed triggers 6-12 requests instead of 1. Crash rate unchanged. Android logs show GET /recs fired in bursts of 3-4 when scrolling. The code:

@Composable
fun RecsCard(vm: FeedViewModel) {
    val recs by vm.recs.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    if (recs == null) vm.loadRecs()          // "only if not loaded"
    recs?.let { RecsRow(it) }
}

loadRecs() launches viewModelScope.launch { _recs.value = api.recs() }. A red herring: the QA lead blames a retry interceptor in OkHttp.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without changing the API contract. How do you prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the OkHttp retry or adds a boolean isLoading flag in the composable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the duplicate request appear without scrolling? (isolates recomposition triggers.) Is the VM scoped to the screen or the activity? Is the Compose compiler reporting RecsCard as skippable? What does the server see for request IDs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side dedupe or a client feature flag disabling the card; a client hotfix that guards loadRecs with an in-VM if (job?.isActive == true) return.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) side effect in composition body, repeated each recomposition while recs == null; (b) OkHttp retry (red herring: retries show identical request ids and timing, ours differ); (c) parent recomposition on scroll; (d) VM recreated.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts on RecsCard during load; log in loadRecs; OkHttp event listener to count calls vs retries; breakpoint on loadRecs to see the call stack is in composition.
  5. Root cause: loadRecs() runs during composition every time recs is still null. Every state read (scroll, loading shimmer, other state) recomposes the card and fires another launch. Since loadRecs has no guard, N recompositions before response = N requests.
  6. Fix: short-term: guard in VM. Long-term: trigger load from the VM init/on first collection (stateIn(WhileSubscribed)), or use LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.loadRecs() } if UI must trigger it.
  7. Prevention: lint (ComposableCallsInEffect-style review rule: no non-composable calls with side effects in the body), a test that recomposes and asserts one call, and request-count assertions in integration tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not add a UI boolean flag: it resets on recomposition entry/leaving and rotation; do not rely on server dedupe forever.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does LaunchedEffect(Unit) fix it fully? → Single run per entry; recomposition doesn't restart it.
  • Still two requests after fix on rotation? → New composition, new effect; VM should dedupe by caching.
  • What if the card scrolls off and back in LazyColumn? → The item is disposed and re-entered; the VM cache should handle it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar bug cost a team a week because the burst was masked by a CDN cache; the symptom was a cost spike on the monthly bill, not a crash.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network layer or adds a UI flag.
  • Hire: finds the call in the body and moves it to an effect or VM.
  • Strong hire: also guards idempotency in the VM, verifies via Layout Inspector counts, adds regression test.

questions.promptHtml: derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, and remember(key) all seem to "compute something from state". How do you choose between them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The three get confused constantly; the answer shows you know the consumer (composition vs coroutine) and the update frequency.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "derivedStateOf makes a State for composition to read that only notifies when the computed result changes, useful when inputs change faster than the output, like scroll offset to a boolean. snapshotFlow turns State reads into a Flow for an effect. remember(key) just caches a value computed from inputs and recomputes when keys change, but it is evaluated during composition so it cannot react to State changes by itself."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tool Consumer Reacts to State read inside? Use when
plain expression composition recomposes the reader output changes as often as input
remember(key){} composition only when keys change; reads inside are not re-evaluated unless the scope recomposes caching an allocation
derivedStateOf composition yes, notifies readers only if result changes input faster than output
snapshotFlow coroutine yes, emits distinct results side effects, debouncing, analytics

derivedStateOf is wrapped in remember normally; without it a new derived state is created each recomposition. It is not free: it has its own observation and cache. Docs warn that combining two states via derivedStateOf (full name) is overhead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val showButton by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } } // composition reads a Boolean
LaunchedEffect(listState) { snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }.collect(::log) } // side effect
val fullName = "$first $last" // not derivedStateOf: updates as often as inputs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• derivedStateOf not wrapped in remember.
  • Passing a changing value as a captured variable into derivedStateOf without keying the remember (stale): use remember(key).
  • Using snapshotFlow to drive UI instead of letting composition read state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. derivedStateOf and a lambda-captured parameter changes? → The cached derived state won't see it; key remember(param) or use rememberUpdatedState.
  2. Cost? → One extra State object and snapshot observer per instance; skip it for 1:1 derivations.
  3. Can derivedStateOf be read in a draw/layout lambda? → Yes and it reads only invalidate that phase.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "derivedStateOf avoids recomposition". Senior: names the consumer, the frequency criterion, and the stale-capture trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wrapping "isError = text.length > 20" in derivedStateOf made typing slightly slower with no recomposition benefit; removing it cleaned the profile.

questions.promptHtml: In what order do effects run relative to composition, and what is the order when keys change or a composable leaves?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ordering explains "why is my listener registered twice" or "why was cleanup after setup" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Effects never run during composition. After a composition pass is applied, the runtime first disposes or forgets effects that left or whose keys changed, then runs onRemembered for new ones (starting LaunchedEffect coroutines), then SideEffect lambdas. A LaunchedEffect coroutine is dispatched, so its body starts after that apply step, not inline. So cleanup of the old always happens before setup of the new."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the runtime's apply step (verify exact internals against your compose-runtime version): leaving RememberObservers get onForgotten (dispatch in reverse order of remembering), entering ones get onRemembered in order, then SideEffects in order. LaunchedEffect.onRemembered calls scope.launch, which the Main dispatcher queues, so the first line of the block executes slightly after apply. Abandoned compositions (never applied) call onAbandoned: effects are never started.

pass N applied:
  1. onForgotten / onDispose   (old effects, children before parents generally)
  2. onRemembered              (LaunchedEffect launch, DisposableEffect block)
  3. SideEffect lambdas
  4. launched coroutines begin on dispatcher

Practical consequence: a parent's SideEffect and child's effects order follows the tree order of registration; do not depend on cross-composable ordering, communicate through state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Order() {
    SideEffect { Log.d("fx", "SideEffect") }
    DisposableEffect(Unit) { Log.d("fx", "Disposable start"); onDispose { Log.d("fx", "dispose") } }
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { Log.d("fx", "Launched body") }
}
// typical first composition log: Disposable start, SideEffect, Launched body

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the LaunchedEffect body runs before the first frame is drawn.
  • Relying on sibling-to-sibling effect order.
  • Reading a View's size in an effect expecting layout to have finished (it may not).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the effect see the new UI? → Yes, the tree is applied; layout/draw may still be pending.
  2. What if composition is abandoned? → Effects never start.
  3. Order between old dispose and new launch on key change? → Dispose first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "after composition". Senior: describes forgotten/remembered/SideEffect phases, dispatch deferral of coroutine start, and avoids cross-effect ordering assumptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A focus request in LaunchedEffect(Unit) crashed with "FocusRequester is not initialized" on slow devices because the modifier was not attached yet; fixed by awaiting a frame.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat list (LazyColumn, ~300 messages) loads link-preview cards. After the backend started prepending new messages at the top, support reports flickering previews and a 3x increase in /preview calls (from ~40k to ~120k per hour, DAU 150k). No crashes. The item code:

LazyColumn {
    items(messages) { msg ->                  // no key
        val preview by produceState<Preview?>(null, msg.url) { value = repo.preview(msg.url) }
        MessageRow(msg, preview)
    }
}

Another suspect: the image loader's disk cache (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Why does inserting at the top cause this, and how do you fix it and verify?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases the disk cache or adds remember around the repository call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Message.id stable and unique? Is the repo call cached? Do previews flicker when prepending only, or also on append? Which Compose version (item key semantics are the same across)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache previews in the repo by URL (in-memory LRU) so repeated calls are cheap, and ship a key fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no key so identity is positional; (b) unstable msg.url key; (c) cache eviction; (d) image loader (red herring since the network call is the preview API).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in the producer and watch calls on prepend; Layout Inspector shows item recomposition; test with a fake repo counting calls.
  5. Root cause: Without keys, LazyColumn identifies items by index. Prepending shifts every message down one index, so each index now hosts a different message: the produceState key msg.url changes at every position, cancelling the in-flight preview and starting a new one (also any remembered state is attached to the wrong message). That is the same "reorder restarts effects" problem the lifecycle docs describe.
  6. Fix: items(messages, key = { it.id }). Now each composable instance and its effect follows the message. Add contentType when row types differ.
  7. Prevention: lint/review rule for lazy lists without keys when items carry state or effects, plus a Compose UI test that prepends an item and asserts the call count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not use index or hashCode as keys; keys must be stable and unique, and in LazyColumn must be Bundle-saveable types for state restoration (verify).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if ids can duplicate? → Crash on duplicate keys in lazy lists; dedupe before.
  • Can I fix it with key(msg.id){} inside non-lazy Column? → Yes, the key composable does the same for regular layouts.
  • Should the load be in the item at all? → Better in a state holder (prefetch), but that is an architecture call.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar prepend regression only showed up in staging with real chat volume; locally the test data never prepended.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames cache or network.
  • Hire: identifies missing keys and fixes.
  • Strong hire: explains positional identity, effect restart mechanics, verifies with a counted test and notes state-saving implications.

questions.promptHtml: How should a Compose screen collect a StateFlow from a ViewModel? Compare collectAsState, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and collecting in LaunchedEffect.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you know Compose does not stop collection when the app is backgrounded unless told.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Plain collectAsState keeps collecting as long as the composable is in the composition, even when the Activity is stopped and in the background, so upstream work (database, location) keeps running. The lifecycle variant collects only while the lifecycle is at least STARTED by default, via repeatOnLifecycle, and pauses otherwise. Collecting inside LaunchedEffect has the same not-lifecycle-aware issue unless I wrap it in repeatOnLifecycle."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: collectAsStateWithLifecycle (androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose, 2.6.0+) creates a State with an initial value and runs lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(minActiveState) in a produceState-like effect. When the lifecycle drops below STARTED, collection is cancelled; for a stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)) upstream, the 5-second timeout then stops the upstream. It re-collects on return and the State holds the last value meanwhile. For a non-StateFlow Flow you must pass an initialValue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: HomeViewModel = viewModel()) {
    val ui by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()   // StateFlow<UiState>
    Content(ui)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using collectAsState in an Android screen and wondering why a location callback continues in the background.
  • Using LaunchedEffect { flow.collect } for events without repeatOnLifecycle.
  • Forgetting WhileSubscribed upstream, so lifecycle awareness gives nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would collectAsState be correct sometimes? → Multiplatform code (no Android lifecycle), or deliberately app-lifetime collection.
  2. Which lifecycle? → LocalLifecycleOwner.current, which is the Activity/Fragment/NavBackStackEntry owner.
  3. Dropped values while STOPPED? → For StateFlow no problem (conflated); for Flow/SharedFlow events they are lost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "the lifecycle one is better". Senior ties it to WhileSubscribed upstream, event loss semantics and nav destination lifecycle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A map screen's fused-location Flow kept running while the app was backgrounded for 20 minutes due to collectAsState; battery team traced the wakelock to it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you handle one-time UI events like navigation or a snackbar in Compose? Compare a Channel/SharedFlow collected in an effect with "event as state that you consume".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: There is no universally agreed answer; interviewers test whether you can articulate the trade-offs and pitfalls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Compose re-reads state on every recomposition, so a one-shot event stored as plain state and never reset fires again on rotation or recomposition. Two approaches: (1) a Channel exposed as Flow from the ViewModel and collected in a lifecycle-aware effect, delivering each event once but risking loss if nobody is collecting; (2) model the event as state in UiState with an explicit onEventConsumed() the UI calls after handling, which is reliable but more boilerplate. The official guidance leans towards state that is consumed; I choose per event criticality."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The old SingleLiveEvent problem moved into Flow: SharedFlow with replay=0 drops events with no collector; Channel(BUFFERED) buffers until collected but delivers to one collector and can lose an event if the collector is cancelled mid-handling (e.g. at the instant of rotation). State-based events survive config change and process-safe if put in saved state, but the UI must consume them exactly once.

Channel/Flow State + consume
Delivery at most once, can be lost at least once until consumed
Rotation risk safe
Boilerplate low higher
Testing collect in test assert state

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// State + consume
data class UiState(val nav: NavTarget? = null)

@Composable
fun Screen(state: UiState, onNavConsumed: () -> Unit, navigate: (NavTarget) -> Unit) {
    val nav = state.nav
    LaunchedEffect(nav) {
        if (nav != null) { navigate(nav); onNavConsumed() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• State flag that is never cleared: navigates twice after rotation.
  • Collecting a Channel with collectAsState.
  • Clearing the event before the navigation actually happened.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why LaunchedEffect(nav) and not Unit? → Need to react to each new event; keyed on the event instance (give events unique ids to allow identical repeats).
  2. Do events belong in UiState? → Many treat them as part of state precisely to avoid loss; this is a debated architecture choice (UDF design in A4).
  3. What about snackbars needing a queue? → Keep a list in state or a Channel with BUFFERED capacity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use SharedFlow/Channel". Senior: names loss modes, rotation, WhileSubscribed, ids for repeated identical events and the consume protocol.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "payment succeeded" navigation was lost when the user rotated precisely as the event emitted; QA reproduced 1 in 200. State-based consume fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (1.2M MAU) has a "transfer" flow. After the transfer API returns, the ViewModel emits NavigateToReceipt via MutableSharedFlow<Event>() (no replay, default buffer). Support tickets: about 0.4% of successful transfers leave the user stuck on a spinner; the money moved. Crash rate is flat. Logs show event emitted but no navigated. Pattern: users who lock the screen or switch apps right after tapping Confirm. Collection code:

LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    vm.events.collect { if (it is NavigateToReceipt) nav.navigate("receipt") }
}

A red herring: a recent OkHttp upgrade (the team's first guess).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, the production impact and how you'd redesign delivery.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switches SharedFlow to replay = 1, which now re-fires the navigation on every new collection (rotation, return).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the collector lifecycle-aware or app lifetime? Which dispatcher does the VM emit on? Is the activity recreated on app switch (process or config)? Does the problem correlate with onStop? Is tryEmit used (drops when no subscriber)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: On resume, the UI reads transfer status from the repository/UiState and navigates if success; ship as a hotfix since money-moved-but-stuck is high severity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) event emitted while no collector (backgrounded, the effect disposed or the composition gone): SharedFlow without replay drops it; (b) collector cancelled mid-handling by rotation; (c) navigation called while the NavController is in a bad state; (d) OkHttp upgrade (red herring: the server response arrives, evidenced by the event emitted log).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with adb shell input keyevent HOME during the call, add logging at collector start/stop, test with a TestScope emitting before collecting; check subscription count (subscriptionCount).
  5. Root cause: A SharedFlow with no replay is hot: if no collector is active at emit time the event is gone. After backgrounding, the composition (or its lifecycle-aware collector) is not active, so the single NavigateToReceipt is lost and UI state never moves past "loading".
  6. Fix: Make completion part of state: UiState.transferResult (Success(receiptId)) so any future collection renders it; UI navigates via LaunchedEffect(result) and calls onResultConsumed(). Short-term: Channel(BUFFERED) with receiveAsFlow() collected under repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), accepting rare loss at the instant of cancellation.
  7. Prevention: instrument "action succeeded but no terminal UI event within N seconds" as a metric; write a test that emits with no collector and asserts delivery on later collection; avoid tryEmit on SharedFlow for important events.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not use replay = 1 (duplicate navigation), do not use a global singleton event bus, do not rely on the UI to re-fetch without idempotency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process death while the API call was in flight? → The repository should persist the transfer result so a restored screen reads it from state, not from an event.
  • Why not SingleLiveEvent? → Same problem class: relies on observer being active; hides lost events.
  • Double navigation after the fix? → The consume callback must clear state before or atomically with navigation, and navigation guarded by the current destination.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team found the bug because the support ticket cluster correlated with "app switched to banking OTP SMS app" exactly at confirmation time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks replay or blames the network layer.
  • Hire: identifies lost event with no collector and moves to state.
  • Strong hire: addresses idempotency, process death, consume semantics, and monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: On what dispatcher does a LaunchedEffect block run, what is special about its context, and how does cancellation behave when keys change mid-operation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level questions probe the runtime, and cancellation bugs (partial writes, double work) are common.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It runs on the composition's effect coroutine context: the Android main dispatcher (a UI dispatcher integrated with Choreographer) plus a MonotonicFrameClock, which is why animations and withFrameNanos work inside. When keys change or the composable leaves, the job is cancelled, which is cooperative: it only stops at suspension points, so non-cancellable or blocking code finishes anyway, and cleanup must use try/finally and withContext(NonCancellable) for suspend calls."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The Recomposer owns an effectCoroutineContext (supplied by AndroidUiDispatcher.Main plus a BroadcastFrameClock-style clock); effects are children of the composition's job via CompositionScopedCoroutineScopeCanceller. withFrameNanos suspends until the next frame callback from Choreographer. Cancellation delivers CancellationException at the next suspension; blocking calls (Thread.sleep, big loops without yield/ensureActive) block the main thread and delay cancellation. Two quick key changes produce: cancel A, start B; A's finally runs before B starts (cancel is requested, but B's launch is dispatched afterwards).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LaunchedEffect(docId) {
    try {
        val doc = repo.load(docId)                // cancellable suspend
        withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { index(doc) }  // CPU off main
    } finally {
        withContext(NonCancellable) { repo.releaseLock(docId) } // must complete
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CPU-heavy parse directly in the block (frame drops).
  • Catching Exception and swallowing CancellationException, so the effect never stops.
  • Assuming a request in flight is aborted: only if the client call is cancellable (Retrofit suspend/OkHttp call cancellation).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does an uncaught exception in an effect crash? → It propagates to the composition's job and crashes the app unless handled (verify with your runtime version for supervisor behavior); catch inside.
  2. Where does withFrameNanos hook? → The composition's MonotonicFrameClock tied to Choreographer.
  3. Test environments? → Use the test dispatcher/ComposeTestRule's mainClock, not real time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "main thread, cancelled on change". Senior: names frame clock, cooperative cancellation, NonCancellable cleanup, swallowed CancellationException bug.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A catch (e: Exception) around a repo call swallowed cancellation, so the old effect kept writing stale results after the user switched documents.

questions.promptHtml: How are LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect implemented, and why do they survive recomposition but not an abandoned composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth: RememberObserver, slot table and apply-phase dispatch.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each is remembered into the slot table at its call site with its keys; the remembered object implements RememberObserver. When the composition is committed the runtime calls onRemembered (start coroutine, run block); when its group is removed or keys change it calls onForgotten (cancel, dispose). If the pass is discarded before commit, onAbandoned is called instead and the effect never started. That is why they are safe where body side effects are not."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
remember(keys){ LaunchedEffectImpl(scope, block) }: key equality decides whether the slot's value is reused. Composer collects RememberObservers during composition into a list; on applyChanges it dispatches onRemembered/onForgotten/onAbandoned and SideEffect callbacks. DisposableEffectImpl.onRemembered runs the block, saving the onDispose handle. Compose also lets you write your own: remember an object implementing RememberObserver to hook lifecycle without coroutines. Positional memoization (group keys plus order) is what ties the instance to the call site.

compose pass --> RememberObservers collected --> commit? yes: onRemembered / onForgotten
                                                       no : onAbandoned (effect never ran)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private class Tracker : RememberObserver {
    override fun onRemembered() { /* acquire */ }
    override fun onForgotten() { /* release */ }
    override fun onAbandoned() { /* never acquired: nothing to release */ }
}
@Composable fun rememberTracker() = remember { Tracker() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Acquiring a resource in the remember lambda constructor (runs during composition, may be abandoned, leaks). Acquire in onRemembered.
  • Assuming onForgotten is called on process death.
  • Conditional calls that move the effect's position (group identity), restarting it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is onAbandoned not the same as onForgotten? → Resource was never acquired.
  2. Does rememberCoroutineScope follow the same model? → Yes, a RememberObserver cancels the scope on forgotten/abandoned.
  3. How does key() interplay? → It changes group identity so effects move with the data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "remember with keys". Senior: RememberObserver lifecycle, abandon path, and resource-acquisition rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom rememberPlayer created ExoPlayer inside remember {}; discarded compositions (fast navigation) leaked decoders until it was moved to RememberObserver.onRemembered.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants "screen viewed" and "item impression" analytics for a feed (2M DAU, avg 25 items viewed per session). Current implementation logs inside each item's LaunchedEffect(item.id), producing 3x over-counting: items re-log when scrolled off and back, on rotation, and when the app returns from background. Data science needs: impression counted once per item per session, only when at least 50% visible for 500 ms. Event volume budget: under 60M/day. Red herring: someone proposes counting in the ViewModel on item load.
questions.promptHtml: Design the tracking. Which effect primitives, where does state live, what do you debounce, and what are the failure modes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use LaunchedEffect per item with delay(500)" with no dedupe across scroll or rotation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "once per session" process or user-visit? Must it survive process death? Is visibility measured by layout (LazyListState.layoutInfo) or by pixels? Is it acceptable to drop on crash? Are events batched?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add server-side dedupe by (session, itemId) to stop the data pollution while the client is fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why current logs are noisy): per-item effects restart on re-entry; no session memory; lifecycle background counts as re-enter.
  4. How I'd verify each: Debug logger counts per item in a QA script (scroll up/down, rotate, background); compare client vs server counts.
  5. Root cause: Item composition lifetime is not a business concept: LazyColumn disposes and recreates items; effects restart with them.
  6. Fix: one effect at list level: LaunchedEffect(listState) with snapshotFlow { listState.layoutInfo.visibleItemsInfo } mapped to ids passing the 50% visibility check, debounced via distinctUntilChanged plus per-id timers (e.g. collectLatest with delay(500) for new ids), a Set<String> of seen ids held in the state holder (survives scroll; saved with rememberSaveable or in the VM for rotation), and events sent to a batched analytics queue. Screen view: LaunchedEffect(Unit) plus lifecycle ON_START re-entry policy decided with product.
  7. Prevention: a unit test of the visibility reducer as a pure function; a dashboard of events per DAU; contract tests that scroll programmatically.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: not logging in onBind/composition; not exact pixel visibility on every frame (cost: snapshotFlow already conflates per frame); accept undercount if the app dies before the batch flushes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if items are reordered by server pushes? → Visibility by id, not index.
  • Multiple lists on one screen? → One tracker per list state or a shared tracker with source tags.
  • Rotation? → Hold the seen set in the ViewModel or rememberSaveable with a listSaver.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team halved analytics cost by moving impression logic from per-item effects to a pure reducer fed by one snapshotFlow; the reducer also made the logic unit-testable without a device.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-item effect with delay.
  • Hire: list-level snapshotFlow, seen-set, debounce.
  • Strong hire: state ownership across rotation, batching, testing as a pure function, and trade-offs on accuracy vs cost.

questions.contextHtml:
A navigation-heavy app (Compose Navigation, 40 destinations) had an incident: battery drain complaints, a 2.1x increase in sensor wakeups, and OOM crashes up from 0.3% to 1.1% of sessions in 3 days. LeakCanary on a debug build reports HomeScreen$...$observer retained by SensorManager. The offending code:

@Composable
fun StepCounter(sm: SensorManager, onSteps: (Int) -> Unit) {
    val listener = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) = onSteps(e.values[0].toInt())
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
    }
    DisposableEffect(Unit) {
        sm.registerListener(listener, sm.getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_STEP_COUNTER), SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_NORMAL)
        onDispose { }
    }
}

Red herring: the team suspects the Navigation library keeps back stack entries too long.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fix, and what process change prevents it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds sm.unregisterListener(listener) to onDispose only, ignoring that the listener captured is the one from the first composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the leak appear when navigating away, or on rotation too? How many screens use this pattern? Is the lambda onSteps capturing a ViewModel or an Activity? Which release introduced it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix to unregister, and a server flag to disable the step counter feature if the release can't go out quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) empty onDispose leaks the listener and captured lambda chain; (b) listener is re-created each recomposition but the effect holds only the first (a mismatch: unregistering listener would not remove the registered first one if the variable changed); (c) Navigation back stack retention (red herring: LeakCanary shows the SensorManager as the GC root path).
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary retained-object trace; dumpsys sensorservice shows registered connections count growing with navigation; heap dump in Android Studio; instrumented test that navigates 20 times and checks listeners.
  5. Root cause: The effect never unregisters (empty onDispose) and the listener is built in the body: a new object each recomposition, while the effect (keyed Unit) registered only the first instance, which captures onSteps, a lambda capturing a screen-scoped object. SensorManager is a system-lifetime root, so each visit leaks the screen subgraph.
  6. Fix: create the listener inside the DisposableEffect, key on sm, read the callback via rememberUpdatedState, and unregister the same instance in onDispose (code below).
  7. Prevention: custom lint/Detekt rule: onDispose {} empty is a warning (the docs call it a smell); LeakCanary on instrumentation tests that traverse navigation; a code-review template item "every register has an unregister on the same object".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: not using a bare Activity-scoped registration, not catching OOM; do not blame navigation without the trace.
@Composable
fun StepCounter(sm: SensorManager, onSteps: (Int) -> Unit) {
    val current by rememberUpdatedState(onSteps)
    DisposableEffect(sm) {
        val listener = object : SensorEventListener {
            override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) = current(e.values[0].toInt())
            override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
        }
        sm.registerListener(listener, sm.getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_STEP_COUNTER), SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_NORMAL)
        onDispose { sm.unregisterListener(listener) }
    }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should this be in a ViewModel? → If steps drive business state, yes: a repository exposing a Flow with callbackFlow and awaitClose.
  • Does callbackFlow solve the same? → Yes, awaitClose is the equivalent of onDispose.
  • What about registering in onStart/onStop instead? → Depends on whether background counting is needed; battery guideline says stop.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The retained subgraph included large bitmaps from an image screen, so the leak masqueraded as an image-loading memory problem for two weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames navigation or adds a random unregister.
  • Hire: moves the listener inside the effect, unregisters the same instance.
  • Strong hire: adds rememberUpdatedState, lint/review prevention, discusses callbackFlow/ViewModel ownership and lifecycle (start/stop).

questions.contextHtml:
A form screen autosaves a draft. Users report that after typing and quickly pressing back, about 2% of drafts are lost (analytics: 18k lost per day at 900k daily saves). Another symptom on QA: "Save" occasionally throws CancellationException in logs. Code:

@Composable
fun DraftScreen(vm: DraftViewModel, onBack: () -> Unit) {
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    var text by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }

    scope.launch { vm.saveDraftDebounced(text) }   // (A)

    TextField(text, { text = it })
    BackHandler {
        scope.launch {                              // (B)
            vm.saveDraft(text)
            onBack()
        }
    }
}

Red herring: the team blames the Room transaction timeout.
questions.promptHtml: List every bug, explain the draft loss mechanically, and produce a fixed design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only notices (A) launches in the body; leaves (B) which cancels with the composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is saveDraft a suspend function on a repository with its own scope? Should the save survive screen exit? What is the debounce policy? Is back handled by nav or this handler?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the final save into vm.saveDraft(text) launched on viewModelScope (or an application scope) and call onBack() right away.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) save coroutine cancelled when the screen leaves the composition on back; (b) body-launched coroutine starts on every recomposition (every keystroke): many racing saves; (c) Room timeout (red herring: no transaction timeout in logs, CancellationException points at cancellation).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log job start/cancel with a name; Layout Inspector counts recompositions; test: type, trigger back, assert repository write count using a fake.
  5. Root cause: (A) is a side effect in composition: every recomposition launches another debounced save, yielding unordered writes. (B) rememberCoroutineScope is cancelled when DraftScreen leaves the composition: onBack() pops the destination, the composition is disposed, and a save still in flight is cancelled; if onBack() runs before save completes (e.g. save is not awaited in the case of scheduling) the result is lost.
  6. Fix: autosave in the ViewModel: text flows into vm.onTextChanged(it) that debounces with viewModelScope (debounce on a Flow); final save on back via vm.onBack() that saves then emits a navigation state; UI collects. Where truly UI-bound, use LaunchedEffect(Unit) { snapshotFlow { text }.debounce(500).collectLatest { vm.save(it) } } and flush in onDispose/VM onCleared through a non-cancellable app scope.
  7. Prevention: test with rapid back, CancellationException metrics, a rule: durable work never lives in a composition-scoped coroutine.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not use GlobalScope; use an injected application scope or WorkManager for guarantees; do not block the UI thread on save.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process death during save? → Persist to Room with a transaction; WorkManager for guaranteed completion.
  • Would NonCancellable inside the scope help? → Only if the composition scope outlives the process work; usually still tied to UI, wrong owner.
  • Why not just runBlocking? → ANR risk.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A notes app lost "last 500 ms of typing" for months; the fix was ownership: the UI observes, the ViewModel owns durability.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sees only the Room red herring.
  • Hire: finds body launch and composition-scoped cancellation, moves to ViewModel.
  • Strong hire: also covers debounce design, durability ownership, tests and process death.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test composables that use LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect or timers, deterministically?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Effects involve time, lifecycle and coroutines, and flaky tests are a senior-level pain point.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use the Compose test rule's virtual clock: composeTestRule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false and advanceTimeBy for delays inside effects, since effect coroutines run on the composition context controlled by the test. For DisposableEffect I toggle a state that removes the composable and assert the cleanup was called on a fake. For lifecycle behavior I use a TestLifecycleOwner provided via CompositionLocalProvider(LocalLifecycleOwner ...). I avoid Thread.sleep and use waitUntil only for real async work."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: createComposeRule() swaps in a test dispatcher and a controllable clock: delays in LaunchedEffect use virtual time linked to mainClock (verify delays use the Compose test clock in your setup; delay inside effects is controlled when the rule's mainClock is driving; with StandardTestDispatcher in UI tests you may need runTest integration). The rule idles between frames; waitForIdle runs pending effects and recompositions. Ordering: compose content, waitForIdle, assert side effect on the fake. For flows, expose a MutableStateFlow in a fake VM and push values.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@get:Rule val rule = createComposeRule()

@Test fun timeoutFiresOnce() {
    var timeouts = 0
    rule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false
    rule.setContent { Splash(onTimeout = { timeouts++ }) } // delay(2_000) inside
    rule.mainClock.advanceTimeBy(1_999)
    assertEquals(0, timeouts)
    rule.mainClock.advanceTimeBy(2)
    assertEquals(1, timeouts)
}

@Test fun disposableUnregisters() {
    val fake = FakeSource()
    var show by mutableStateOf(true)
    rule.setContent { if (show) Listen(fake) }
    assertEquals(1, fake.listeners)
    show = false
    rule.waitForIdle()
    assertEquals(0, fake.listeners)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Real delay with Thread.sleep in tests.
  • Asserting immediately after setContent; effects have not run.
  • Testing effects only in the happy path, not recomposition with changed params (stale capture) or key change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test recomposition did not restart the effect? → Counter in a fake incremented in the effect block; recompose with new params; assert 1.
  2. Idling for Retrofit? → Use fakes or IdlingResource.
  3. Testing lifecycle collection? → Provide a LifecycleOwner you can move to STARTED/STOPPED.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: waitForIdle and sleeps. Senior: virtual time, fakes with counters, lifecycle owner injection, and tests for restart/stale-capture semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky splash test (15% failure in CI) became deterministic by switching to mainClock.advanceTimeBy, cutting CI reruns.

questions.contextHtml:
A feed restores scroll position after process death and also syncs "last read index" to the server. Complaints: on cold start after process death, the list jumps to the top 8% of the time, and the server receives writes 4x a second while scrolling (server rate-limit alerts, 429s at 0.7%). Code:

@Composable
fun Feed(vm: FeedViewModel) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val lastRead = vm.lastRead   // plain Int property read once

    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { listState.scrollToItem(lastRead) }

    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }
            .collect { vm.syncLastRead(it) }
    }
    LazyColumn(state = listState) { /* items from vm.items */ }
}

Items load asynchronously (p95 400 ms). Red herring: suspected rememberLazyListState saver bug.
questions.promptHtml: Find every defect and give the corrected design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay before scrollToItem" or "use rememberSaveable for index".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is lastRead from server or local? Do items exist when the first effect runs? Is sync intended per item or throttled? Should rotation restore through listState's saver or the VM?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle server writes with debounce(1000) server-side flag first; disable restore if it mis-scrolls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) scrollToItem fires before items are loaded: index out of range of an empty list clamps to 0; (b) sync emits every index change, no debounce; (c) lastRead read once (plain), not reactive; (d) rememberLazyListState saver (red herring: it restores on rotation but the effect then overrides it).
  4. How I'd verify each: log layoutInfo.totalItemsCount at scroll time; count syncLastRead calls per second; unit test with a fake loading delay.
  5. Root cause: The restoration effect runs on first composition when the list is empty, so scrollToItem has nothing to scroll to; and it re-runs on every cold start, overriding the saved scroll state restored by rememberLazyListState (a double owner of position). The sync collects every index change with no debounce or distinctUntilChanged on a coarse bucket.
  6. Fix: key the restore on data availability: LaunchedEffect(items.isNotEmpty()) { if (items.isNotEmpty() && !restored) listState.scrollToItem(...); restored = true } held in rememberSaveable; use a single owner for position (either listState saver or VM). Sync: snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }.debounce(1_000).distinctUntilChanged().collect(vm::syncLastRead), keyed on listState.
  7. Prevention: tests with delayed data; metrics for sync rate per user; rate-limit alerts correlated to releases.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not sync on every frame; do not mix two sources of scroll truth; do not use fixed delays to wait for data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not collectLatest? → For a fire-and-forget sync, collect with debounce is enough; collectLatest cancels an in-flight sync when a new index arrives.
  • Is firstVisibleItemIndex read in composition OK? → Reading in an effect avoids recomposition per scroll.
  • Flush on stop? → Add a lifecycle ON_STOP flush so the final index is not lost to debounce.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A news app's "resume reading" had a 6% mis-restore rate caused purely by race ordering between restore and first page load.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds fixed delay.
  • Hire: waits for data via key, debounces sync.
  • Strong hire: single source of position, lifecycle flush, and tests with delayed items.

questions.contextHtml: Product: "make search-as-you-type feel instant but don't hammer the backend." Search API p95 is 350 ms, capacity budget is 5 req/s per user, typical typing speed is 5 chars/s, 400k DAU with 30% using search. The current code calls vm.search(q) in onValueChange, producing about 5 req/s per active user and out-of-order results (result for "andr" shown after "android" 3% of the time). The PM also says "results must never be stale" and "show results within 300 ms of the last keystroke".
questions.promptHtml: Design the effect-based pipeline in Compose, resolve the conflicting requirements, and explain where each piece lives.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: delay(300) inside onValueChange launched via a new scope per keystroke (old ones never cancelled).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "never stale" mean: no out-of-order or max age? Is a 300 ms debounce plus 350 ms latency acceptable (650 ms to results)? Should short queries (1 char) search? Cache hits?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop out-of-order results by cancelling previous requests (client side).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The issues are concurrency (no cancellation), no debounce, and ordering; the red herring is "backend too slow".
  4. How I'd verify each: Log request start/finish with query seq; Perfetto/OkHttp event listener for concurrent calls; test with a fake repo that delays earlier queries longer.
  5. Root cause: Each keystroke starts independent work, results race.
  6. Fix: Keep text state hoisted.
