Effect: LaunchedEffect(vm) { snapshotFlow { text }.debounce(250).filter { it.length >= 2 }.distinctUntilChanged().collectLatest { q -> vm.search(q) } }, or do it in the ViewModel with flatMapLatest. collectLatest/flatMapLatest cancels the previous request when a new query arrives, guaranteeing order. Show the previous results with a loading indicator (stale-while-revalidate) rather than clearing. Latency trade: 250 debounce plus 350 backend = 600 ms; to meet "within 300 ms" I'd add a local/cached prefix result immediately.
  7. Prevention: a fake-clock test that types "a-n-d" with delays and asserts a single call; a metric for requests per search session.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not remove debounce entirely (capacity), do not clear the list on each keystroke (flicker), do not put the debounce in the TextField's onValueChange (state must update immediately to keep typing smooth).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should debounce be in UI or ViewModel? → ViewModel for testability and survival of config change; UI-level snapshotFlow acceptable for purely UI state.
  • IME composition text? → Debounce on committed text; TextFieldValue composing region (verify behavior for CJK).
  • Cancel on lifecycle stop? → Yes via collectAsStateWithLifecycle upstream or repeatOnLifecycle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A marketplace cut search traffic by roughly 55% with a 250 ms debounce plus flatMapLatest, with no measurable change in conversion, and removed the out-of-order ticket class entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: delays per keystroke without cancellation.
  • Hire: debounce plus collectLatest/flatMapLatest, hoisted text.
  • Strong hire: negotiates the requirements with numbers, stale-while-revalidate, caching, placement and tests.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review for a release candidate of a settings screen (screen recompositions are reported high; scroll jank 9% of frames over 16 ms on a mid-range device). The PR contains several effect uses:

@Composable
fun SettingsScreen(vm: SettingsViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    var filtered by remember { mutableStateOf(emptyList<Setting>()) }

    LaunchedEffect(state.query, state.items) {          // (1)
        filtered = state.items.filter { it.name.contains(state.query) }
    }
    LaunchedEffect(state.darkMode) {                    // (2)
        AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode(if (state.darkMode) MODE_NIGHT_YES else MODE_NIGHT_NO)
    }
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.refresh() }               // (3)
    Button(onClick = { /* ... */ }) {
        LaunchedEffect(Unit) { analytics.log("button_shown") }   // (4)
    }
    DisposableEffect(Unit) { onDispose { } }            // (5)
    SettingsList(filtered)
}
questions.promptHtml: Review it. Which effects are wrong, why, and what do you change? Rank by production impact.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, maybe add keys"; or rewrites everything without ranking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is filtered used elsewhere? Is refresh() idempotent? Who owns night mode (the VM or an app theme store)? How many items (n)? Does analytics.log belong to the item or the screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; request changes before merge. If shipped, feature-flag the filter path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked by impact: (1) derived state held in an effect = an extra recomposition per change plus one frame of stale UI (filtered lags the query); jank source when n is large. (2) Night mode set from an effect can recreate the Activity; ownership belongs outside composition. (3) Likely fine but refresh() runs again after rotation; idempotency must be checked. (4) Logging inside a Button's content lambda ties the event to composition of a tiny node; meaning is unclear and can re-fire if the button re-enters. (5) Empty onDispose is pointless.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector counts (settings list recomposes twice per keystroke), Perfetto frame timeline, compiler report for SettingsList params.
  5. Root cause: Effects used as a state-sync mechanism ("when A changes, set B"), which adds a composition pass (state write after composition, then recomposition) and a frame of inconsistent UI. Effects should connect Compose to the outside world; derivations belong in the composition or ViewModel.
  6. Fix: (1) val filtered = remember(state.query, state.items) { state.items.filter { it.name.contains(state.query, true) } }, or do it in the ViewModel for big lists. (2) VM exposes the setting; apply the night mode in the Application/Activity once, not per recomposition of a screen. (3) keep with idempotent refresh or move into VM init. (4) Log from the screen-level effect or click handler. (5) delete it.
  7. Prevention: review checklist "before writing an effect: is this an event handler, a derivation, or a real external connection?"; Compose lint; baselines of recomposition counts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not reflexively wrap the filter in derivedStateOf (inputs change as often as output); do not move all effects to the ViewModel blindly; some UI-only effects (focus, scroll) belong in Compose.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Filter of 5k items per keystroke on main thread? → Move to VM combine on Dispatchers.Default and debounce.
  • Is remember(keys) enough with a mutable list inside state? → Only if the list instance changes or the list is a snapshot list read in the lambda.
  • Why is the effect-based filter a frame late? → The effect runs after composition is applied; its state write triggers a second composition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replacing three "sync state in an effect" blocks with plain derived values removed one full frame of lag and cut recomposition counts per interaction in half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts all effects or only adds keys.
  • Hire: identifies effect-as-derivation and body/VM ownership problems.
  • Strong hire: ranks by impact, explains the extra-pass mechanism, checks idempotency and ownership, adds review checklist.
